subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 4-day-old boy born at home after an uncomplicated pregnancy is brought for persistent oozing from the umbilical stump and a small hematoma at the site of a heel stick. He is exclusively breastfed and did not receive any injections after birth. Examination is otherwise normal. Laboratory studies show a prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, a normal bleeding time, a platelet count of 245,000/mm3, and a normal fibrinogen level.
question: Deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's bleeding?
explanation_correct: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and on proteins C and S. Newborns have sterile intestines and cannot synthesize the vitamin, and breast milk is a poor source, so deficiency in the first days of life causes hemorrhagic disease of the newborn with prolonged PT and aPTT, a normal bleeding time, and normal platelets; an intramuscular dose at birth prevents it.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vitamin C is required for collagen hydroxylation and causes scurvy with perifollicular and gingival bleeding, but it does not prolong the prothrombin time.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hemophilia A prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time only; the prothrombin time and bleeding time remain normal.
explanation_incorrect.D: von Willebrand disease typically prolongs the bleeding time with a normal or mildly prolonged aPTT and a normal PT, reflecting a primary hemostatic defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a platelet aggregation defect with mucosal bleeding and a prolonged bleeding time but normal coagulation studies and a normal platelet count.

educationalObjective: Neonates require parenteral vitamin K at birth because sterile intestines and poor breast-milk content leave them deficient in vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
